ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Acute shortness of breath with sharp right-sided pleuritic back pain; onset this morning without obvious trigger. Two brief episodes of haemoptysis.  
• Symptom timeline and progression: Sudden onset today of pain on deep inspiration and breathlessness. Low-grade subjective fever noted. Two-week history of fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance; otherwise previously well.  
• ENT symptoms: Denies throat tightness, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor, noisy breathing or facial/lip/tongue swelling. No ear pain, hearing change, neck pain or neck swelling.  
• Relevant past episodes/treatments: None reported. No prior similar haemoptysis, no prior emergency visits for breathing issues.  
• Allergies: None known (medications, food, environmental).  
• Current medications: Methotrexate – dose/route/frequency not documented; last taken this morning. No rescue inhalers or antihistamines.  
• Past medical history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). No history of VTE, recent travel or surgery.  
• Social context: 45-year-old female; non-smoker; desk job; lives alone in a flat; owns a cat; speaking from private location.

Objective:
• Observable swelling/distribution: None; face, lips, tongue and neck appear normal on video.  
• Airway/breathing: No stridor or increased work of breathing observed. Able to speak full sentences.  
• Mental status: Alert and oriented.  
• Vitals/exam findings: Radial pulse regular 66–74 bpm. Capillary refill normal. Oropharynx unremarkable; no cervical lymphadenopathy. Temperature, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation not recorded.  
• Presence of another person: None (patient alone).

Assessment:
Working impression: Likely community-acquired pneumonia with haemoptysis in immunosuppressed host (methotrexate), requiring in-person chest examination and vitals. Patient currently clinically stable on video review.

Supporting evidence: Acute fever, pleuritic chest/back pain, cough with blood-streaked sputum, shortness of breath, immunosuppression due to methotrexate.

DDx (aligned with transcript and DDx list):
1. Community-acquired pneumonia – high likelihood; classic triad of fever, pleuritic pain and haemoptysis; immunosuppression increases risk.  
2. Pulmonary embolism – medium likelihood; pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis and SLE-related hypercoagulability, but normal heart rate and no provoking factors oppose.  
3. Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis/alveolar haemorrhage – lower likelihood; on methotrexate, but presentation usually subacute and typically produces dry cough; fever less typical.

Plan:
• Same-day face-to-face GP clinic review arranged for full vital signs, chest auscultation, blood pressure and temperature measurement.  
• Possible chest X-ray and blood tests based on in-person findings; consider sputum culture if productive cough.  
• Antibiotic therapy anticipated if pneumonia confirmed; no drug prescribed at this stage.  
• Escalation instructions: Call emergency services immediately for worsening breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up larger amounts of blood, dizziness/syncope, high fever or new voice change/throat tightness.  
• Avoid NSAIDs and continue methotrexate unless advised otherwise after assessment.  
• Follow-up: Post-clinic update via telehealth or in-app messaging; consider outpatient chest imaging if symptoms persist or red flags emerge.  
• Patient reassured that presentation less suggestive of lung cancer; longer-term imaging may be requested if no improvement.

Quality checks:  
● Missing/expected elements: Full vital signs (BP, RR, SpO₂, temperature); lung auscultation; detailed methotrexate dose and adherence; documented allergy list beyond “none”; prior pneumococcal/influenza vaccination status; availability of emergency contact.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; both sources prioritize pneumonia vs. PE.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; minor conversational digressions but clinical data understandable.
